q.q: Which is the best description of the purpose of a computer program?
o: A set of instructions the computer executes to carry out a specific task
A diagram showing the steps of a solution before it is turned into code
The physical components of the computer that process and store the data
A logical plan for a task that is written before any code is produced
q.why: A program is software: instructions executed to perform a task. A logical plan written first is an algorithm; physical parts are hardware.

q.q: A spreadsheet package is an example of...
o: an operating system
a utility program
a hardware component
an application program
q.why: It carries out a particular job for the user, so it is an application program.

q.q: An antivirus scanner keeps a computer system running well. Which kind of program is it?
o: An application program
An operating system
A utility
An algorithm
q.why: Utilities perform housekeeping tasks such as backup, antivirus scanning and file compression.

q.q: Which kind of program manages the hardware and provides an interface so that the user and other programs can use the computer?
o: Utility
Operating system
Application program
Compiler
q.why: The operating system (e.g. Windows, macOS, Android) manages the hardware and provides an interface.

q.q: Why is an algorithm normally designed before a program is written?
o: Algorithms run faster than the programs written from them
The computer needs the flowchart in order to run the code
The logic can be planned and checked before time is spent coding
Programs cannot contain loops unless an algorithm exists
q.why: The computer has no common sense to fill gaps, so the logic is planned first; errors found in design are cheaper to fix.

q.q: A self-service checkout looks up the price of each scanned barcode and adds it to a running total. In the input – process – output pattern, this lookup and adding is the...
o: input
output
process
storage
q.why: Barcodes are input, looking up prices and totalling is processing, and the itemised receipt is output.

q.q: Which is the best definition of an algorithm?
o: A set of instructions that a computer executes to carry out a specific task
A diagram that uses standard symbols to show the steps in a solution
A structured, code-like version of English used to plan a program
A finite, ordered sequence of precise and unambiguous steps that solves a problem
q.why: That is the notes' definition. The first distractor defines a program; the others describe a flowchart and pseudocode.

q.q: The step 'repeat until the bread is golden' most clearly risks breaking which property?
o: Finiteness
Efficiency
Precision of inputs
Having an output
q.why: If the condition is never met the loop never ends, so the algorithm may not terminate.

q.q: 'Turn at the church' on a road with two churches breaks which property of a good algorithm?
o: Unambiguous
Ordered
Efficient
Finite
q.why: The step can be read two ways, so it is ambiguous.

q.q: The instruction 'wait a bit for the register' breaks which property?
o: Precise
Finite
Ordered
Efficient
q.why: Each step must say exactly what to do, e.g. 'wait 2 minutes', not vague quantities or times.

q.q: How many inputs and outputs must an algorithm have?
o: At least one input and at least one output
Exactly one input and exactly one output
At least one input and zero or more outputs
Zero or more inputs and at least one output
q.why: An algorithm may have no inputs (e.g. print the 7 times table) but must produce at least one related output.

q.q: In a fire drill, one person checks all 900 pupils instead of each teacher checking their own class. Which property does the single-checker version lack?
o: Finiteness
Efficiency
Unambiguity
Ordering
q.why: Efficient algorithms avoid unnecessary steps or needlessly slow methods.

q.q: A program asks for a quantity and the user types a letter. According to the notes, what should a correct and effective algorithm do?
o: Treat the letter as zero and carry on with the calculation
Produce a clear message rather than crash or give a wrong answer
Stop the program immediately so no wrong answer is given
Ignore the input and use the previous value instead
q.why: Invalid input should produce a clear message, not a crash or a silently wrong answer.

q.q: What is decomposition?
o: Breaking a complex problem into smaller sub-problems
Removing detail that is not relevant to the problem
Working through an algorithm by hand step by step
Repeating a set of steps until a condition is met
q.why: Decomposition = take apart. Removing irrelevant detail is abstraction.

q.q: A designer splits a school canteen system into 'top up account', 'order meal' and 'print receipt'. This is...
o: abstraction
iteration
decomposition
a dry run
q.why: Splitting a problem into sub-problems is decomposition.

q.q: A sat-nav map shows roads and junctions but not individual houses. This is an example of...
o: abstraction
decomposition
selection
iteration
q.why: Unneeded detail has been removed, leaving a simpler model: abstraction.

q.q: For a bike-hire app, which data would abstraction most likely leave out?
o: The dock location of each bike
The battery level of each bike
The frame colour of each bike
The ID number of each bike
q.why: Abstraction keeps essential data (dock location, battery level, bike ID) and leaves out detail such as frame colour or saddle height.

q.q: What diagram is used to show the result of decomposition?
o: A structure diagram
A flowchart
A trace table
A Gantt chart
q.why: A structure (top-down) diagram shows the whole problem at the top and smaller tasks underneath.

q.q: Which is a benefit of decomposition?
o: Sub-problems can be developed and tested by different programmers
It removes the need to design an algorithm at all
It means the program needs less data to be stored
It always makes the finished program run faster
q.why: Separate modules can be shared out and tested independently. Needing less data is a benefit of abstraction.

q.q: In a decomposed design, what does each bottom-level task usually become in the final program?
o: A module, such as a procedure or function
A variable in the main program
A flowchart decision symbol
A row in the trace table
q.why: Each bottom-level task usually becomes a module (procedure or function).

q.q: Which flowchart symbol is used for 'INPUT value'?
o: Parallelogram
Rectangle
Rounded rectangle
Diamond
q.why: Inputs and outputs use a parallelogram. Using a rectangle for input or output loses marks.

q.q: Which flowchart symbol is used for a yes/no test?
o: Diamond
Parallelogram
Rectangle
Rounded rectangle
q.why: A decision is a diamond with two labelled exits.

q.q: What is shown by a rounded rectangle on a flowchart?
o: START or END
A calculation
An input or output
A decision
q.why: The terminator is a rounded rectangle used for START and END.

q.q: Which loop is most suitable when the number of repetitions is known before the loop starts?
o: WHILE
REPEAT…UNTIL
IF…THEN…ELSE
FOR (count-controlled)
q.why: A count-controlled FOR loop is used when the number of repetitions is known; WHILE and REPEAT are condition-controlled.

q.q: What is the difference between a WHILE loop and a REPEAT…UNTIL loop?
o: WHILE tests last and runs at least once; REPEAT tests first and may run zero times
WHILE is count-controlled, while REPEAT…UNTIL is condition-controlled
WHILE tests first and may run zero times; REPEAT tests last and runs at least once
WHILE can only be used in pseudocode; REPEAT…UNTIL can only be used in flowcharts
q.why: A WHILE loop tests the condition first; REPEAT…UNTIL tests it at the end, so its body always runs once.

q.q: A key advantage of pseudocode over a flowchart is that it...
o: can be run directly by the computer without translation
is quicker to write and translates more directly into code
is visual and easy to follow for people without training
is tied to one language, so there is no ambiguity
q.why: Pseudocode is compact and close to code, but it cannot be executed directly. Flowcharts are the visual option.

q.q: In the café algorithm, purchase values are read until -1 is entered. The values 3, 7, 5, -1 are input in turn. What are the outputs for total and bigSpends (purchases of £5 or more)?
o: 15 and 1
15 and 2
14 and 2
15 and 3
q.why: total = 3 + 7 + 5 = 15; 7 and 5 are >= 5, so bigSpends = 2. The -1 is the sentinel and is not added.

q.q: In the café algorithm, what is the purpose of the value -1?
o: It is a negative purchase that is added to the total
It is the starting value of the running total
It is a boundary value used to test the condition
It is a sentinel value that signals the end of the input
q.why: A sentinel value marks the end of the data and is not processed as data.

q.q: What is a dry run?
o: Working through an algorithm by hand, step by step, exactly as written
Running the compiled program with test data on the computer
Checking that the code follows the language's syntax rules
Working through the algorithm as the designer meant it to work
q.why: A dry run follows the algorithm exactly as written, not as the designer intended, recording values in a trace table.

q.q: Why can a compiler not detect a logic error?
o: Logic errors stop the program before it is compiled
The code is still valid syntax; it just produces the wrong result
Logic errors only ever occur in pseudocode, not code
The compiler ignores IF statements and loops
q.why: Logic errors are valid code with faulty reasoning, so they compile and run.

q.q: In a trace table, when is a new row written?
o: Each time values change
Once for each line of code
Only when there is an output
Only at the end of the loop
q.why: A new row is written whenever values change, so every pass of a loop is visible.

q.q: A loop should run for days 1 to 7 but uses WHILE day < 7, starting from day 1. What happens?
o: It runs 7 times
It runs 6 times
It runs 8 times
It runs forever
q.why: Days 1–6 satisfy day < 7, so only 6 passes: an off-by-one error.

q.q: For a test 'age >= 18', which pair is the best boundary data?
o: 18 and 30
5 and 50
17 and 18
q.why: Boundary data sits either side of the edge of the condition.

q.q: An algorithm sets max ← 0, then reads four temperatures and keeps the highest. With readings -3, -1, -7, -2, what is output?
q.why: No reading is greater than 0, so max is never changed: a logic error caused by the starting value.

q.q: A condition-controlled loop has no INPUT inside it, so its condition never changes. What logic error results?
o: An off-by-one error
A syntax error
An infinite loop
An uninitialised total
q.why: If the condition can never change, the loop never ends.

q.q: In an algorithm that adds up a list of numbers, the output is printed after every number instead of once at the end. What is the likely cause?
o: The total was not initialised to zero
The output statement is placed inside the loop
The loop uses < where <= was needed
The total is reset to zero inside the loop
q.why: Output placed inside the loop is printed on every pass instead of once.

q.q: What must be true of a list before a binary search can be used?
o: It must contain no duplicates
It must contain fewer than 1000 items
It must be stored in a serial file
It must be sorted
q.why: Binary search relies on order to know which half to discard.

q.q: In a binary search, low = 5 and high = 8. What is mid?
q.why: (5 + 8) DIV 2 = 13 DIV 2 = 6, rounding down.

q.q: When does a binary search conclude the target is not present?
o: When the middle item is larger than the target
When mid becomes equal to zero
When low becomes greater than high
When low becomes equal to high
q.why: low > high means no items remain. When low = high there is still one item to check.

q.q: A linear search is carried out for 'Newry' in the list Omagh, Derry, Newry, Bangor. How many comparisons are made?
q.why: Omagh, Derry, then Newry matches on the third comparison and the search stops.

q.q: In a binary search, the item at mid is smaller than the target. What happens next?
o: high ← mid − 1
low ← mid
high ← mid + 1
low ← mid + 1
q.why: If the target is larger, it can only be in the upper half, so low moves past mid.

q.q: A binary search is carried out on the sorted list 1004, 1011, 1019, 1023, 1030, 1042, 1057, 1063, 1078 (positions 0 to 8) for 1063. Which items are compared, in order?
q.why: mid = 4 (1030), then low = 5, mid = 6 (1057), then low = 7, mid = 7 (1063) found.

q.q: Which statement about linear search is correct?
o: It works on any list, sorted or not
It only works on lists that are sorted
It always checks every item in the list
It discards half of the list each time
q.why: Linear search checks each item in turn until a match or the end, and works on unsorted data.

q.q: Why is binary search called a divide and conquer algorithm?
o: Each comparison throws away half of the remaining items
It divides the list into single items and merges them
It splits the work between several processors
It compares each item with its neighbour in turn
q.why: Each comparison discards the half that cannot contain the target.

q.q: What does (3 + 8) / 2 evaluate to in C# when both values are int?
o: A compile error
q.why: int / int is integer division: 11 / 2 = 5.

q.q: Why does LinearSearch return -1 when the target is absent?
o: -1 is the index of the last item in every array
-1 can never be a valid array index, so it signals 'not found'
Returning -1 stops the whole program immediately
C# methods must always return a negative number
q.why: Indexes start at 0, so -1 is an unambiguous 'not found' value.

q.q: A programmer writes while (low < high) in a binary search. What is the effect?
o: The search turns into a linear search of the array
The method sorts the array before searching it
The search works exactly the same as with <=
When low equals high, the last remaining item is never checked
q.why: A one-item range has low = high, which would be skipped, so the condition must be low <= high.

q.q: Why must a binary search set high = mid - 1 rather than high = mid?
o: Otherwise the range may not shrink, and a search for a missing value can loop forever
Otherwise the middle item would be compared twice, giving the wrong index
Otherwise integer division would round the midpoint up instead of down
Otherwise the method would return -1 even when the target is present
q.why: Moving past mid guarantees the range shrinks each pass, so the loop always terminates.

q.q: In the C# LinearSearch method, what is the effect of return i; inside the for loop?
o: The loop continues to check the rest of the list
The method returns the index of the last match
The loop restarts from the first index again
The method ends immediately at the first match
q.why: return ends the method immediately, so the search stops at the first match.

q.q: The array towns = { "Coleraine", "Strabane", "Banbridge", "Larne", "Dungannon" } is searched with LinearSearch(towns, "Larne"). What is returned?
q.why: Indexes start at 0: Coleraine 0, Strabane 1, Banbridge 2, Larne 3.

q.q: Why can a C# binary search on sorted strings not compare a[mid] < target directly?
o: Strings cannot be stored in a sorted array in C#
The < operator compares string lengths, not order
Binary search can only be used on integer arrays
C# does not allow < with strings; string.Compare or CompareTo is used
q.why: Comparing strings with < is not allowed in C#; string.Compare(a[mid], target) or CompareTo is used instead.

q.q: Why is efficiency measured by counting comparisons rather than timing the program?
o: Timing a program is impossible in C#
Comparisons always take exactly one second
Comparisons do not depend on the speed of the particular computer
Big-O notation only applies to timings
q.why: A count reflects the algorithm, not the hardware.

q.q: What is the worst-case number of comparisons for a binary search of 100 sorted items?
What is the worst-case number of comparisons for a binary search of 1000 sorted items?
What is the worst-case number of comparisons for a binary search of 5000 sorted product codes?
q.why: 2¹² = 4096 ≤ 5000 < 8192, so the worst case is 12 + 1 = 13.

q.q: A linear search is O(n). If the list grows from 2000 to 4000 items, what happens to the worst-case comparisons?
o: They increase by one
They double
They quadruple
They stay the same
q.why: Linear growth: doubling n doubles the work.

q.q: A binary search is O(log n). If a sorted list doubles from 1 million to 2 million items, what happens to the worst-case comparisons?
o: They double
They halve
They increase by one
They stay the same
q.why: In logarithmic time doubling n adds only one comparison: 20 becomes 21.

q.q: What is the average number of comparisons for a successful linear search of n items?
o: About log₂ n
Exactly n
Exactly 1
About n/2
q.why: On average the target is found halfway through the list.

q.q: An algorithm takes 3n + 2 steps. How is its time complexity written in Big-O notation?
o: O(n²)
O(n)
O(log n)
q.why: Big-O ignores constant factors and smaller terms; only the dominant term n matters.

q.q: Which situation best suits a linear search?
o: An unsorted list of 15 items searched once
A sorted dictionary used by a spell-checker
A sorted list of 2 million postcodes searched constantly
A sorted product database held in an array
q.why: Small, unsorted and searched once: there is no benefit from sorting first.

q.q: Why might a binary search be unsuitable for records read one at a time from a serial file?
o: Records in a serial file can never be sorted
Binary search needs direct access to the middle item
Binary search only works on text, not records
Serial files are always too small to benefit
q.why: Jumping to the middle requires direct (random) access; serial files are read in sequence.

q.q: A list is unsorted and will be searched only once. Why is binary search a poor choice?
o: Binary search would need more memory than the list itself
Binary search cannot find numbers in an unsorted list quickly
Binary search is slower than linear search on any list
The cost of sorting first outweighs the saving from one fast search
q.why: Sorting takes far more work than a single linear search.

q.q: Which conditions best justify using a binary search?
o: Large, sorted data with direct access that is searched many times
Small, unsorted data that is searched only once
Large data read one record at a time from a serial file
Data that arrives constantly in a random order
q.why: Binary search pays off on large, sorted, directly accessible data searched frequently.

q.q: New items arrive constantly in random order and must be searched. What is the hidden cost of using a binary search?
o: Keeping the list sorted costs time on every addition
Each search must check every item in the list
The search can only be used on serial files
Each new item doubles the worst-case comparisons
q.why: Inserting each new item in its correct place costs time on every addition.

q.q: Why is linear search sometimes chosen even though binary search is faster on large lists?
o: It always makes fewer comparisons on any list
It needs the list to be sorted before it is used
It is simple to code, with little risk of off-by-one errors
It needs direct access to the middle of the list
q.why: Linear search is simple; binary search is more complex, with a risk of off-by-one errors in low, high and mid.

q.q: Large real systems often use indexes, hash tables or tree structures. Which principle do they share with binary search?
o: Checking every record in turn from the start of the file
Reducing the number of comparisons needed to locate a record
Sorting the data again before every single search
Reading the records one at a time in sequence
q.why: They follow the same principle as binary search: reduce the comparisons needed to find a record.

q.q: How does a bubble sort work?
o: It inserts each item into its correct place in a growing sorted section
It splits the list into single items and merges the sorted sub-lists
It compares adjacent pairs and swaps them if they are in the wrong order
It partitions the list around a pivot and sorts each side recursively
q.why: Bubble sort compares adjacent items and swaps them, pass after pass. The others describe insertion, merge and quick sort.

q.q: After the first pass of an ascending bubble sort, what is guaranteed?
o: The smallest item is in its final position at the start
The first two items are sorted relative to each other
The largest item is in its final position at the end
No further swaps will be needed on later passes
q.why: The largest value is carried to the end on pass 1.

q.q: Why is a temporary variable needed when swapping two array elements?
o: To count how many swaps have been made
To stop one value being overwritten and lost
To store the length of the list being sorted
To record whether the list is now sorted
q.why: Without temp, the first assignment overwrites a value before it is copied.

q.q: What is the list 9, 4, 7, 2 after one pass of an ascending bubble sort?
What is the list 31, 18, 25, 7, 42, 12 after the first pass of an ascending bubble sort?
q.why: 31 is swapped past 18, 25 and 7, stops at 42, then 42 is swapped with 12, giving 18, 25, 7, 31, 12, 42.

q.q: In the bubble sort pseudocode, why is end reduced by 1 after each pass?
o: The list gets one item shorter as items are removed
It stops the sort as soon as a pass makes no swaps
The last item of each pass is already in its final place
It makes the next pass start one place further along
q.why: Each pass carries the largest remaining value to the end, so later passes can stop one place earlier.

q.q: The C# bubble sort uses do { ... } while (swapped); to match REPEAT…UNTIL swapped = False. Why is the condition reversed?
o: Repeating while swapped is the same as repeating until not swapped
C# does not allow the value False in a loop condition
A do…while loop tests its condition before the body runs
The C# version sorts the list into descending order
q.why: Both loops run the body at least once; 'repeat while swapped' and 'until not swapped' are equivalent.

q.q: In an insertion sort of 8, 3, 5, 1, what is the list after the first pass?
q.why: Key 3 is inserted before 8; the rest is untouched. 3, 5, 1, 8 is a bubble sort pass.

q.q: In an insertion sort of 8, 3, 5, 1, what is the list after the second pass?
q.why: Key 5 is inserted between 3 and 8, so the first three items are in order.

q.q: How many passes does an insertion sort make on a list of 10 items?
o: It depends on the data
q.why: One pass for each item except the first: n − 1, always.

q.q: Why does j >= 0 come before heights[j] > key in the while condition of the C# insertion sort?
o: C# evaluates conditions from right to left
Short-circuit evaluation stops heights[-1] being accessed
It makes the sort put items in descending order
It is purely a style choice with no effect
q.why: If j < 0 the second test is skipped, avoiding an out-of-range error.

q.q: During an insertion sort of 31, 18, 25, 7, 42, 12, the key on pass 3 is 7. Which items are shifted right?
o: 31 only
31 and 25
None of them
q.why: Before pass 3 the sorted section is 18 25 31; all three are larger than 7 so all are shifted.

q.q: In an insertion sort, what happens when the key meets an item that is not larger than it, or the start of the list?
o: The two items are swapped
The key drops into the gap
The pass is repeated
The sort stops completely
q.why: Larger items are shifted right; the key is then inserted into the gap.

q.q: Which list is best suited to an insertion sort?
o: A very large list in random order
A list too big to fit in memory
A list in reverse order
A small or nearly sorted list
q.why: On nearly sorted data very few shifts are needed; a reversed list is its worst case.

q.q: What is merged at the first merging stage of a merge sort?
o: The two halves of the original list
The pivot with each half
Adjacent swapped items
Pairs of single-item lists
q.why: After splitting down to single items, pairs of single items are merged first.

q.q: To merge two sorted lists, what does merge sort do?
o: Compares the front items and moves the smaller into the result, repeatedly
Compares the back items and moves the larger into the result, once only
Chooses a pivot and places smaller items to its left, larger to its right
Swaps each adjacent pair that is out of order until no swaps are made
q.why: Compare front items, move the smaller, repeat; when one list empties, copy the rest of the other.

q.q: In a merge sort of 27, 12, 41, 8, 33, 19, 50, 4, what are the four sorted pairs after the first merge?
q.why: Each pair of adjacent single items is merged into order: 27/12, 41/8, 33/19, 50/4.

q.q: In quick sort, what is true of the pivot after partitioning?
o: It is removed from the list
It is in its final sorted position
It moves to the start of the list
It is always the median value
q.why: Everything smaller is left of it and everything larger is right, so it is in place.

q.q: Quick sort is applied to 27, 12, 41, 8, 33, 19, 50, 4 with the first item as pivot. Which items end up to the left of the pivot?
o: 4, 8 and 12 only
q.why: The pivot is 27; the items smaller than 27 are 12, 8, 19 and 4.

q.q: When does quick sort perform worst?
o: When the pivot always splits the list evenly
When the pivot is repeatedly the smallest or largest item
When the list has an even number of items
When the list is in a random order
q.why: Unbalanced partitions remove one item at a time, giving O(n²).

q.q: What is the main drawback of merge sort?
o: It is O(n²) in the worst case
It cannot sort lists of odd length
It only works on lists of numbers
It needs extra memory for the sub-lists
q.why: Merging needs extra storage roughly the size of the list, so it does not sort in place.

q.q: Which sort guarantees O(n log n) time whatever the order of the input?
o: Quick sort
Insertion sort
Merge sort
Bubble sort
q.why: Merge sort always splits evenly. Quick sort can degrade to O(n²) with poor pivots.

q.q: A list of 500 000 items is already almost in order, with two items out of place. Which sort would perform well?
o: Quick sort with a first-item pivot
Bubble sort without a flag
Quick sort with a last-item pivot
Insertion sort
q.why: Insertion sort is close to O(n) on nearly sorted data; quick sort with a first-item pivot would be near its worst case.

q.q: Which algorithm is least suitable when memory is very limited?
o: Merge sort
Bubble sort
Insertion sort
Quick sort
q.why: Merge sort needs extra storage for the sub-lists; the others sort in place.

q.q: For n = 1000, roughly how many steps does an O(n²) sort take compared with an O(n log n) sort?
o: About 1 000 000 compared with about 1000
About 1 000 000 compared with about 10 000
About 10 000 compared with about 1 000 000
About 2000 compared with about 10 000

q.q: Why might a simple sort be quicker than merge sort for a list of ten items?
o: It has O(n log n) time complexity, the same as merge sort for all lists
Merge sort cannot be used on a list with fewer than a hundred items
It has less overhead, and the difference in growth is trivial for ten items
Simple sorts use extra memory, which makes them faster on short lists
q.why: For ten items the difference is trivial and a simple sort has less overhead.

q.q: Data is too big to fit in memory and predictable performance matters. Which sort do the notes recommend?
o: Quick sort
Merge sort
Insertion sort
Bubble sort
q.why: Merge sort is guaranteed O(n log n) and merging works well on data read in sequence.

q.q: A large list held in memory must be sorted as fast as possible. Which choice do the notes recommend?
o: Quick sort with a sensible pivot choice
Bubble sort with a swapped flag
Insertion sort with a key
Merge sort with a first-item pivot
q.why: Quick sort is often the fastest general-purpose sort with a sensible pivot. Merge sort does not use a pivot.

q.q: When does a bubble sort with a swapped flag stop?
o: When the flag becomes True
After exactly n − 1 passes
When a complete pass makes no swaps
When the largest item reaches the end
q.why: No swaps in a pass means every adjacent pair is in order.

q.q: How many comparisons does a flagged bubble sort make on an already sorted list of 8 items?
q.why: One pass of n − 1 = 7 comparisons, no swaps, then stop.

q.q: The swapped flag improves which case of bubble sort?
o: Only the worst case, with reversed data
The best case, with sorted or nearly sorted data
The memory used by the sort in every case
None; it only makes the code clearer
q.why: A reversed list still needs every pass; sorted or nearly sorted lists finish early.

q.q: A flagged bubble sort is run on the nearly sorted list 4, 7, 9, 15, 12, 20. How many passes does it make?
q.why: Pass 1 swaps 15 and 12; pass 2 makes no swaps, so the sort stops.

q.q: With a swapped flag, what is the best-case time complexity of bubble sort?
o: O(n²)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
O(n)
q.why: One pass of n − 1 comparisons on a sorted list is O(n) rather than O(n²).

q.q: Which design feature improves a linear search on sorted data when the target is absent?
o: Stop once an item larger than the target is passed
Move low or high to mid plus or minus one
Reduce the end of each pass by one place
Set a flag to True whenever a swap is made
q.why: On sorted data, once a larger item is passed the target cannot be later in the list, so absence is detected early.
